name: House of Terror Museum
description: The House of Terror at Andrássy út 60 is a museum and memorial to the victims of the fascist and communist regimes in 20th-century Hungary, in the building used by both the Arrow Cross and the ÁVH.

children.text: The House of Terror stands at Andrássy Avenue 60. In the 20th century the building was used by two oppressive regimes: the Arrow Cross Party, the Hungarian fascists, and the ÁVH, the communist state security police. It opened as a museum on 24 February 2002, after a foundation bought the building in December 2000 and carried out a year-long renovation.

The interior, the exhibition halls and the facade were designed by Attila Ferenczfy-Kovács. The black structure framing the building, with its blade-like walls, is intentionally stark among the pale facades of Andrássy Avenue, and photographs of victims are displayed on the outside.

The permanent exhibition covers Hungary's relations with Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union and the Arrow Cross and ÁVH years, and it serves as a memorial to the people who were detained, interrogated, tortured or killed in the building. In the basement you can see reconstructed cells like those the ÁVH used for prisoners. A T-55 tank is also displayed, carrying photographs of victims of Hungarian communism.

The museum's presentation has been discussed by historians; some critics argue that it presents Hungary mainly as a victim of foreign occupiers and gives too little attention to Hungarians' own roles in those regimes. It is a good idea to read other sources on the period and treat the museum as one perspective on a contested history.
The subject matter is serious and some displays are disturbing, so allow time and consider whether the visit is suitable for young children.
Good to know
Check the current opening days, ticket types and exhibition status on the museum's official website before your visit.
Some displays are disturbing: consider whether the visit suits younger children.
Andrássy Avenue is a UNESCO-listed boulevard; Oktogon and the Opera House are within walking distance.

historyIntro: The House of Terror is a memorial museum at Andrássy Avenue 60, confronting the violence and political repression of Hungary's twentieth century.

historySections.heading: A building marked by two dictatorships

children.text: The address is associated with the Arrow Cross period and the communist-era political police. The institution presents the experience of people persecuted, imprisoned and tortured under dictatorial regimes.

historySections.heading: Turning a difficult history into public memory

children.text: The building was acquired for a memorial museum in 2000, renovated and opened to the public in February 2002. The exhibitions are intended to communicate the human effects of state terror and should be visited with sensitivity to the victims.

name: House of Unicum
description: A visitor centre in the old Zwack distillery at Dandár utca 1, telling the story of Unicum, the Hungarian herbal liqueur. It combines period bottles, documents and family photographs with a 270-degree film, and visitors can see the old distillery and the cellar where the drink matures in oak barrels.

children.text: The House of Unicum is at Dandár utca 1 in District IX and tells the story of Unicum and the Zwack family. The exhibition shows period bottles, documents, family photographs and relics, with QR codes that link to descriptions, videos or extra images. A 270-degree film interpreted by the Zwack family tells the brand's story, and the old distillery building shows the production technology and the medicinal herbs and spices used in the drink.

Unicum is a herbal liqueur with a recipe based on more than 40 herbs and spices, aged in oak barrels. According to a legend that Wikipedia and other sources repeat, the drink dates from 1790, when the court physician Dr Zwack offered it to Emperor Joseph II, who exclaimed 'Das ist ein Unikum!' (this is unique). It is a story told about the origin of the name, and Wikipedia presents it as legend rather than verified history. The documented firm is dated to 1840, when József Zwack founded the company; the first factory was on Váci utca in Budapest, and in 1892 the company moved to its headquarters on the Danube in Ferencváros. The name Unicum was officially registered on 22 May 1883, together with the round bottle with a red cross that is still used.

The 20th century was turbulent for the family. The distillery was bombed four times in 1944, according to a McDaniel College account of a visit, and after the war the Communist state confiscated the factory. The Zwack family went into exile, while a state-run version was produced from a false recipe. Family members rebuilt production in Italy, and Péter Zwack returned to Hungary in the late 1980s; in 1992 he established the Zwack Unicum company and restored production to the original family recipe.

The visit includes the old distillery, which shows how the drink is made, and the cellar. According to the McDaniel account, Unicum ages for six months in oak barrels, and visitors can taste it on draught. A sample shop sells the full range of products and Unicum souvenirs. Today the range also includes variants such as Unicum Plum, which was introduced in 2012.
Good to know
The visitor centre is at Dandár utca 1 in Ferencváros; check the museum's official page for directions and the nearest public transport.
Visits are built around a guided tour and tasting, so check the official site for current tour times, languages and booking arrangements.
Because the tasting involves a strong alcoholic drink, plan the rest of your day accordingly.
Sources describing the legend and the family history differ in some dates, so treat the exhibition itself as the authority on the story.

historyIntro: The House of Unicum introduces the history of the Zwack family business and the changing fortunes of a distinctive Hungarian herbal spirit.

historySections.heading: A family business in Hungarian industry

children.text: The Zwack name became closely associated with Unicum and its herbal-liqueur tradition. The company has passed through very different political and economic periods, providing an unusual window into the country's modern industrial and family-business history.

The visitor exhibition presents advertising, family objects and the product's heritage alongside the story of its manufacture. The tasting experience is separate from the wider historical value of the museum, and participation should always be an individual choice.

name: Underground Railway Museum
description: A museum inside a disused stretch of the original 1896 tunnel beneath Deák Ferenc tér. Three historic carriages from the M1 line stand on the old tracks, alongside plans, maps and models, and a Zsolnay-tiled 'Gizella tér' sign in the entrance hall recalls the line's first city-centre terminus.

children.text: The Underground Railway Museum, also known as the Millennium Underground Museum, sits under Deák Ferenc tér in central Budapest and is reached through the pedestrian subway that links the square to Deák Ferenc tér metro station. It occupies a tunnel that once carried the tracks of Line M1, which opened on 2 May 1896 in Hungary's millennium year and which the operator BKV describes as the first underground railway on the continent.

The line was built from 1894 to 1896 using the cut-and-cover method, with the Hungarian subsidiary of Siemens & Halske commissioned to construct it. It was meant to bring passengers to City Park along Andrássy Avenue without surface traffic spoiling the street. The original line was 3.7 kilometres long with 11 stations. According to Wikipedia, the original station under Deák Ferenc tér lay only about 2.7 metres below the surface and sat on a sharp curve, so in the 1950s the route was diverted, leaving a stretch of the old tunnel (put at about 60 metres by Hungarian Wikipedia and an industrial-heritage listing, and at 80 metres by English Wikipedia) empty and walled off. The same source says that in the 1960s plans to fill it in gave way to a proposal for a metro exhibition.

The museum opened in 1975, on 26 October according to Wikipedia although one tourism site says 28 October, with three historic carriages lowered into the tunnel by crane, and it was renewed in 1996 for the line's centenary. The vehicles are No. 1, a metal-clad motor car from 1896 shown as it was when withdrawn in 1973; No. 19, a wooden-clad motor car from 1896 restored to its original condition; and No. 81, a driving trailer from 1960. On the platform opposite are relics, plans, maps, photographs and models that trace the history of the line, with a final section on the later metro lines.

Details in the entrance hall repay a look. The name Gizella tér, in Zsolnay glazed tile, comes from the line's original city-centre terminus, which is now Vörösmarty tér station, and panels list people who helped build the railway. A marble plaque records that Emperor Franz Joseph rode the line in 1896 and approved naming it after him. The line you can ride today runs between Vörösmarty tér and Mexikói út.
Good to know
Enter through the pedestrian subway between Deák Ferenc tér and the metro station on that square.
After the museum, ride Line M1 itself between Vörösmarty tér and Mexikói út to see the line the museum celebrates.
Check the operator BKV's official page for current opening times and tickets, and for temporary exhibitions.
The museum's site lists a children's corner and a shop, which may help if you are visiting with a family.

historyIntro: Budapest's underground railway museum tells the story of an urban transport innovation created for a rapidly modernising capital.

children.text: The first line of the Budapest underground opened in 1896, serving the boulevard and celebrations of the Hungarian millennium. It was a landmark in continental European electric rapid transit and remains integral to the identity of Andrássy Avenue.

historySections.heading: A museum inside the old tunnel

children.text: A reconstruction of Deák Ferenc Square station in 1955 left a section of the earlier tunnel unused. The museum opened there in 1975, preserving transport equipment and original historical context below today's busy interchange.

name: Szamos Chocolate Museum
description: A small private museum above a Szamos café-shop on Kossuth Lajos tér, across from Parliament. Assembled by the Szamos family over about thirty years, it follows chocolate from cocoa to bar through moulds, pots, tins and marzipan sculptures. The official Szamos site lists it with guided tours booked online, but check current details before visiting.

children.text: The Szamos Chocolate Museum in Budapest is a private museum on the upper floor of a Szamos shop and café at Kossuth Lajos tér, on the corner across from the Parliament building. The venue described here is the one at Kossuth tér; Szamos has other shops and workshops elsewhere, which are separate venues. The Budapest Times reports that the museum was assembled over about 30 years and opened in 2016, and the official Szamos site lists it as a visitor attraction with online-booked guided tours; a visitor guide updated in October 2026 also describes it as operating, but check the official site for current details before planning a visit.

The collection was built up by Gabriella Szamos and her husband Gyula Kelényi, and the exhibition was compiled by the cocoa expert Anikó S. Nagy. According to a 2017 description and a visitor guide updated in October 2026, a guided tour runs through six rooms and follows chocolate from cocoa cultivation to moulding. There is a Biedermeier-style Sweet Salon about chocolate habits in the 18th and 19th centuries, with chocolate pots, cups and porcelain, and a workshop with working historical machines such as a milk separator and a chocolate mixer. According to the official Szamos site, visitors can also try making a chocolate product and take it home.

The objects on display include moulds for chocolate figures, coffee and chocolate sets, promotional items and a gallery of decorated metal chocolate boxes. Marzipan features prominently, including a large marzipan replica of Jean-Étienne Liotard's painting The Chocolate Girl, about 78 kilograms according to the Szamos site. The Budapest Times also mentions marzipan models of the Parliament building and the Hungarian crown jewels.

The museum is also a window into a family business. Mátyás Szamos (1918–2002) was born Mladen Szavits and grew up in the Serbian community of Szentendre. He began an apprenticeship in 1935 at the József Auguszt confectionery, and a visiting Danish confectioner taught him to make marzipan roses, which became his trademark. The first Szamos shop in downtown Pest opened in 1987, he received the Order of Merit of the Republic of Hungary in 1999, and the company's main base is in Pilisvörösvár. The business is now run by the third generation of the family.
Good to know
The museum is at Kossuth Lajos tér, in front of the Parliament building, so it fits easily with a visit to Parliament.
Guided tours are booked online through the official Szamos site. The museum's page offers guided tours with online time-slot booking; check it for tour languages and group arrangements.
Do not confuse it with other Szamos shops or sites in the region; this entry covers only the Budapest museum at Kossuth tér.
The tour is described as including tastings of chocolate, so check the official site for details of what is included.

historyIntro: The Szamos Chocolate Museum places Budapest's love of confectionery in the setting of an exhibition devoted to chocolate and traditional sweetmaking.

children.text: The museum near Kossuth Square introduces chocolate as a craft and cultural product rather than simply a dessert. Its displays draw on the traditions of Hungarian confectioners and the changing objects associated with making and enjoying sweets.

A visit is a reminder that family businesses, recipes, shop design and packaging can be part of a city's story. Exhibition formats and any tastings can change, so contemporary programme information should be checked separately.
